questions.prompt: How does a SwiftUI List handle large collections of data efficiently?

options.text: By allocating memory and rendering views only for visible rows.
options.explanation: Right. List loads lazily and recycles offscreen rows.

options.text: By converting all data items into static bitmap images on launch.
options.explanation: List renders live dynamic views, not pre-rendered static images.

options.text: By capping the total collection size to twenty items maximum.
options.explanation: List handles thousands of items with smooth 120fps scrolling.

options.text: By offloading all row rendering to background worker threads.
options.explanation: UI view rendering must always execute on the main thread.

questions.prompt: Which protocol allows a model to be used in a List without specifying an id key path?

options.text: Comparable, which defines ascending sort order for row items.
options.explanation: Comparable sorts items but does not provide unique identity.

options.text: Identifiable, which guarantees a stable id property on the model.
options.explanation: Right. Identifiable provides a unique id that List uses automatically.

options.text: Codable, which allows the model to serialize into JSON strings.
options.explanation: Codable handles serialization, not SwiftUI list row identity.

options.text: Equatable, which compares whether two instances share properties.
options.explanation: Equatable checks equality, while Identifiable tracks unique identities.

questions.prompt: Where must the .onDelete modifier be placed to enable swipe-to-delete in a List?

options.text: Directly on the outermost List container view struct.
options.explanation: List does not conform to DynamicViewContent and lacks onDelete.

options.text: On the navigation title modifier attached to the window.
options.explanation: Navigation title sets window titles, not row deletion actions.

options.text: On the ForEach view struct nested inside the List container.
options.explanation: Right. ForEach conforms to DynamicViewContent and supports onDelete.

options.text: On the global App struct inside the application main file.
options.explanation: Row deletion modifiers attach to view loops, not app delegates.

questions.prompt: What issue happens when using id: \.self with an array containing duplicate items?

options.text: The Swift compiler throws an unrecognized key path syntax error.
options.explanation: id: \.self is valid syntax and compiles without error.

options.text: SwiftUI reverses the entire collection on every second scroll pass.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not reverse collection order when duplicates occur.

options.text: The entire view hierarchy is converted to an eager ScrollView.
options.explanation: Duplicate IDs break diffing, not the underlying container type.

options.text: Duplicate IDs break row animations and cause visual display glitches.
options.explanation: Right. Non-unique IDs confuse diffing, breaking animations and deletes.

questions.prompt: Why is declaring var id: UUID { UUID() } as a computed property problematic?

options.text: A new UUID is generated on every redraw, destroying row identity.
options.explanation: Right. Unstable IDs break scroll state, animations, and diffing.

options.text: Computed properties are unsupported by the Identifiable protocol.
options.explanation: Identifiable allows computed properties if they return a stable ID.

options.text: UUID values cannot be converted into 64-bit integer values.
options.explanation: UUID is a standard type that conforms to Hashable cleanly.

options.text: It forces SwiftUI to convert the view struct into a reference class.
options.explanation: Computed properties on structs do not turn them into classes.

questions.prompt: How does a ScrollView with a standard VStack differ from a List?

options.text: ScrollView only supports horizontal scrolling on iOS devices.
options.explanation: ScrollView supports both vertical and horizontal scrolling.

options.text: ScrollView with a VStack loads all child views eagerly in memory.
options.explanation: Right. VStack loads all views immediately, while List loads lazily.

options.text: List does not allow buttons or tap gestures inside its rows.
options.explanation: List supports buttons and interactive gestures normally.

options.text: ScrollView automatically recycles cells like UIKit table views.
options.explanation: A standard ScrollView with VStack does not recycle offscreen views.

options.text: .scrollConfiguration(_:), which controls friction physics.
options.explanation: scrollConfiguration is not a standard SwiftUI list modifier.

options.text: .listStyle(_:), which applies styles like .plain or .insetGrouped.
options.explanation: Right. .listStyle applies platform list styles like insetGrouped.

options.text: .tableViewType(_:), which selects UIKit table view bridges.

options.text: .slideButton(action:), which attaches an arrow icon to the row.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses .swipeActions for custom row actions.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI know which row to animate when an item is removed from a List?

options.text: It checks memory pointer addresses of the row views on the heap.
options.explanation: Views are structs on the stack, not objects with pointer addresses.

options.text: It matches the stable id of each element before and after the change.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI uses stable element IDs to calculate diffs and animations.

options.text: It scans row strings using optical character recognition on the GPU.
options.explanation: SwiftUI diffs structural identity in code, not GPU screen pixels.

options.text: It prompts the user to confirm the index of the deleted row item.
options.explanation: Animations are automated by the diffing engine without user prompts.

options.text: Because List crashes if rows contain more than one text label.
options.explanation: List handles complex composite rows with multiple labels easily.

options.text: Because LazyVStack omits list separators and customizes row layout.
options.explanation: Right. LazyVStack provides lazy loading without default table styling.

options.text: Because LazyVStack supports UIKit Auto Layout constraints directly.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in memory and performance between List and a ScrollView with a standard VStack. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that List uses lazy loading and row recycling for visible cells.
Explains that ScrollView with a standard VStack creates all row views eagerly upon loading.
Mentions that eager loading with large collections causes memory spikes and frame drops.

questions.modelAnswer: List is designed for high performance by creating and recycling views lazily. It only allocates memory for rows that are currently visible on the screen. In contrast, a ScrollView with a standard VStack creates all child view structs eagerly upon loading. For large datasets, eager loading causes high memory consumption and dropped animation frames during scrolling.

questions.prompt: Why is declaring a computed property like var id: UUID { UUID() } dangerous in an Identifiable model? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a computed property generates a new UUID on every access or redraw.
States that unstable IDs prevent SwiftUI from correctly tracking item identities during diffing.
Mentions negative consequences such as broken scroll positions, glitchy animations, or state loss.

questions.modelAnswer: Declaring id as a computed property generates a brand new UUID every time the property is accessed. Because the ID changes on every redraw, SwiftUI treats existing rows as completely new items. This unstable identity breaks SwiftUI's diffing engine, causing row animations to glitch and resetting user scroll positions. To keep identity stable, always declare the identifier as a stored property like let id = UUID().

questions.prompt: Why does attaching .onDelete directly to a List fail to compile, and how do you fix it? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that .onDelete is defined on DynamicViewContent, which List does not conform to.
States that ForEach conforms to DynamicViewContent.
Explains that the fix is to attach .onDelete directly to the ForEach inside the List.

questions.modelAnswer: Attaching .onDelete directly to a List causes a compiler error because .onDelete is an extension on DynamicViewContent. In SwiftUI, List is a container view and does not conform to DynamicViewContent. Instead, ForEach conforms to this protocol to handle collection mutations. To fix this error, wrap your row views inside a ForEach and attach the .onDelete modifier directly to that ForEach block.

questions.prompt: Explain what risks occur when using id: \.self on an array of non-unique elements. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that duplicate items in the collection will produce identical ID values.
States that identical IDs confuse SwiftUI's view identity and diffing algorithm.
Describes the resulting bugs: wrong item deletions, visual glitches, or broken row selections.

questions.modelAnswer: Using id: \.self means each element uses its own value as its identifier. If the array contains duplicate elements, multiple rows share the exact same ID. This confuses SwiftUI's diffing algorithm because rows lose unique structural identity. As a result, deleting one row may remove the wrong item, selection states will break, and animations will glitch. Always make sure IDs are unique or wrap data in an Identifiable model.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI use Identifiable conformance to optimize list updates and animations? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Identifiable provides a stable, persistent key for each item in the dataset.
Explains that SwiftUI matches IDs across render passes to determine insertions, deletions, and moves.
States that stable identity allows SwiftUI to animate only changed rows without redrawing the whole list.

questions.modelAnswer: Conforming a model to Identifiable provides a stable, unique ID for every item in the dataset. When the collection updates, SwiftUI compares the new items against the old ones by their IDs. This allows the framework to determine exactly which rows were inserted, deleted, or moved. Because identity remains stable, SwiftUI animates only the changed rows smoothly without rebuilding the entire list.
